classification_signals: Chapter title 'Maritime Psychology: Definition, Scope and Conceptualization' (p. 14)
Preface states 'This is a research volume that brings together organisational, social and health psychology research concerned with the maritime.' (p. 5)

Chapter explicitly offers 'a definition of maritime psychology, and then sketch the scope of the area, identifying different aspects of the interplay between the study of the maritime and the study of psychology.' (p. 14)
Presents a 'broader conceptualization of the maritime transport industry, using a systems perspective' (p. 14)

Includes 'Table 1 Classification of maritime activities that share and have some distinct psychological attributes' (p. 16) and 'Fig. 1 A nested model of the psychosocial and organisational aspects of maritime work' (p. 21), indicating framework development.
Discusses 'Some Challenges and Opportunities for Maritime Psychology' and previews other chapters (p. 21, 25).

limitations: The volume is not exhaustive or comprehensive, but illustrative of research and practice in maritime psychology (p. 15).
The scope of psychology in the commercial transport sector remains quite underdeveloped (p. 19).
Individual psychological interventions can be counterproductive if implemented in a fundamentally unfair and exploitive working environment, individualizing a systems problem (p. 20).
Seafarers' unions are often reluctant to address exploitative working conditions due to fear of job loss (p. 20).
Interventions focused on individuals without systemic change may be ineffective, or worse, by attributing system failures to individuals (p. 21).
Modelling human behaviour under situations of extreme stress is complex and difficult to predict (p. 22).
Evacuation models may not adequately consider the frailty, mobility, cognitive, or sensory impairments of elderly passengers (p. 22).
The piracy study had a small sample size (25 seafarers) and found no relationship between subjective stress descriptions and age, rank, or length of service (p. 22).
Stigma discourages seafarers from seeking mental health consultation due to fear of losing jobs or not being rehired (p. 23).
The indirect effect of PsyCap on safety climate via job satisfaction was evidenced only for European and not for Filipino crew, highlighting cultural differences (p. 24).

The MMPI-2 study had a relatively small sample size, very few female officers, came from only one company (potentially affecting results due to organizational culture), and had limited access to demographic data (p. 227).
The MMPI-2 study was conducted during a period of financial crisis in Greece, which may have impacted test results (p. 227).
The maritime audience is often in a state of heightened alertness and vigilance to risk, making communication challenging (p. 192).
It is difficult to accurately determine if anyone in the audience is traumatized, necessitating the inclusion of peripheral route cues in communication (p. 194).
Peripheral communication effects are temporary and require repetition; central cues can be introduced as time from an incident elapses (p. 196).
The Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM) has been critiqued for being difficult to test and falsify, and for failing to provide clear guidelines on argument strength (p. 197).
No experimental research testing ELM-based message design in maritime situations was found in the literature (p. 196).
Research in sailing as an intervention is in its infancy, often piecemeal, opportunistic, and of modest scale (p. 232).
More robust research, including randomized controlled trials and longitudinal studies, is needed for sailing as an intervention (p. 232).
The mechanisms of benefit for corporate sailing interventions are not systematically researched (p. 232).
Sailing as an intervention faces challenges such as its perception as elitist and costly, and the removal of therapeutic boundaries familiar to practitioners (p. 232).
A code of good practice and guidance mechanism for practitioners in adventure therapy (including sailing) is needed (p. 232).
The potential for sailing interventions depends on accurately assessing participants' ability to engage and learn, requiring development of assessment tools (p. 232).
minimum_safe_summary: This chapter introduces maritime psychology as the study of human behavior in the maritime environment, emphasizing its growing recognition due to psychosocial factors. It defines the field's scope, primarily focusing on commercial transport, and highlights challenges such as the impact of larger ships and reduced manning on social affiliation, and the counterproductive nature of individual interventions without systemic change in exploitative environments. The chapter also discusses the psychological consequences of piracy, the role of organizational culture and psychological capital in safety, and the potential of positive psychology and sailing as therapeutic interventions. Key limitations include the underdeveloped state of psychology in commercial transport, the complexity of modeling human behavior under extreme stress, and the need for more robust, culturally sensitive, and systems-based research approaches.
